questions.stem: In VCE Geography, a disaster is best defined as:
options: the potential for a natural or human process to cause harm to people or to the environment
a hazard that has been classified by its cause as either geological or hydro-meteorological
a serious disruption to a community's functioning, with human, material, economic or environmental losses
any natural event of very high magnitude, whether or not it affects any people or their property in any way
questions.explanation: A disaster is defined by its impact on a community, not by the size of the event. The potential to cause harm is the definition of a hazard, which may never become a disaster.

questions.stem: Which of these hazards is classified as geological (geophysical)?
options: a storm surge
a malaria outbreak
an oil spill
a landslide
questions.explanation: Geological hazards come from Earth's surface and internal processes, such as earthquakes, volcanic activity, erosion and landslides. A storm surge is hydro-meteorological, malaria is biological and an oil spill is technological.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of a biological hazard?
options: a radiation leak from a power plant
an outbreak of a water-borne disease
a tsunami striking a low coastline
a bushfire in dry eucalypt forest country
questions.explanation: Biological hazards include infectious diseases, animal-transmitted and water-borne diseases, and plant and animal invasions. A bushfire is hydro-meteorological and a radiation leak is technological.

questions.stem: Forest is cleared from a catchment for farming. Afterwards, rain of the same intensity produces larger, faster floods downstream. Under the study design's classification, flooding primarily caused by land clearance is:
options: a biological hazard, because it follows the loss of vegetation
a hydro-meteorological hazard only, because rain is the sole cause
a technological hazard, because it is human induced
a geological hazard, because it reshapes the river valley
questions.explanation: The study design lists flooding primarily caused by land clearance among technological (human-induced and exacerbated) hazards. Rain is not the sole cause here, since the same rain produced smaller floods before the forest was cleared.

questions.stem: Heavy monsoon rain floods a valley, and the saturated hillsides then give way in landslides. In terms of the interconnection between hazards, the landslides are:
options: a primary hazard, because they directly destroy buildings
a technological hazard, because they follow a natural one
a biological hazard, because they strip vegetation from slopes
a secondary hazard generated by the primary flood hazard
questions.explanation: A secondary hazard is triggered by a primary one: here the rain and flooding saturate slopes and set off landslides. Directly destroying buildings does not make a hazard primary, because secondary hazards also cause direct damage.

questions.stem: In March 2011 the Tōhoku earthquake off Japan generated a tsunami that flooded the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant, leading to releases of radiation. This sequence best shows that:
options: tsunamis are hydro-meteorological hazards caused by storms at sea
the greatest impacts of an earthquake always occur at its epicentre
one hazard event can trigger secondary hazards of quite different types
technological hazards occur only where geological hazards are completely absent
questions.explanation: A geological event (the earthquake) caused a tsunami, which in turn caused a technological hazard (the radiation release). A tsunami is geological, because it is set off by sudden displacement of the sea floor rather than by weather.

questions.stem: Most of the world's active volcanoes and largest earthquakes are located:
options: along tectonic plate boundaries, especially around the Pacific
in the stable interiors of the world's largest continental plates
along the Equator, where Earth's crust is at its thinnest
near the poles, where the weight of ice cracks the crust
questions.explanation: Volcanoes and earthquakes are concentrated where plates meet, and the Pacific 'Ring of Fire' holds most of them. Plate interiors are relatively stable, which is why Australia has fewer large earthquakes than New Zealand or Japan.

questions.stem: Tropical cyclones form over:
options: cold ocean currents off the west coasts of continents
warm tropical oceans, but not right at the Equator
hot inland deserts within the tropics of the world
the Equator itself, where the sea is at its warmest
questions.explanation: Cyclones need warm sea water, generally above about 26.5 °C, to supply energy and moisture. They do not form within about 5° of the Equator because the Coriolis effect there is too weak to start the storm spinning.

questions.stem: Which hazard event occurs at the largest spatial scale?
options: a drought affecting much of south-eastern Australia
a landslide that blocks one mountain road in Gippsland
a storm surge that floods one coastal town's foreshore
an oil spill confined to a single harbour in Victoria
questions.explanation: Observational scale refers to the size of the area affected, from local to global. A drought across south-eastern Australia is regional to national in scale, while the other events affect one local site.

questions.stem: For most natural hazards, the relationship between the magnitude of events and their frequency is that:
options: magnitude and frequency rise together, so large events become routine
low-magnitude events occur far more often than high-magnitude events
high-magnitude events occur more often because they release more energy
events of every magnitude occur with about the same frequency over time
questions.explanation: Magnitude and frequency are inversely related: small earthquakes, floods and storms are common, while very large events are rare. Releasing more energy does not make an event more frequent; it usually takes longer for that energy to build up.

questions.stem: The moment magnitude scale is logarithmic. An earthquake of magnitude 7.0 releases roughly how much more energy than one of magnitude 5.0?
options: about 20 times
about 2 times
about 1000 times
about 100 times
questions.explanation: Each whole step on the scale releases about 32 times more energy, so two steps is about 32 × 32 ≈ 1000 times. The figure of 100 times is the increase in measured ground-motion amplitude (10 × 10), not in energy.

questions.stem: Which of these describes a role that floods play in natural systems?
options: preventing native fish from breeding in the river's billabongs
depositing nutrient-rich silt that renews floodplain soils
permanently removing all organic matter from the wetlands
lowering the water table across the surrounding valley
questions.explanation: Floods spread silt and nutrients across floodplains and refill wetlands, which is why floodplains are often fertile. Many native fish, such as golden perch, spawn in response to rising flows rather than being prevented from breeding.

questions.stem: Many Australian eucalypts resprout from buds under their bark after fire, and some plants release seed only after being burnt. In geographic terms this shows that bushfire:
options: occurs only in places where there is no human settlement nearby
plays a role in natural systems to which many species have adapted
is a biological hazard rather than a hydro-meteorological hazard
has no negative impacts at all in Australia's natural environments
questions.explanation: Fire is part of many Australian ecosystems, and species such as eucalypts and banksias have adaptations that depend on it. That does not make fire harmless: very frequent or intense fires can still destroy habitat and kill wildlife.

questions.stem: Farmers continue to cultivate the slopes of active volcanoes such as Mount Merapi in Java, despite the risk of eruptions. The main reason is that:
options: eruptions there occur only about once every thousand years
lava flows are slow enough to be stopped by farmers
weathered volcanic material forms highly fertile soils
volcanic slopes are protected from all other hazards
questions.explanation: Volcanic ash and rock weather into fertile soils, a long-term positive impact that draws dense farming populations. Merapi is one of Indonesia's most active volcanoes, so its eruptions are frequent rather than once in a millennium.

questions.stem: Which set of conditions most increases the risk of a fast-spreading bushfire?
options: low temperature, low humidity, still air and sparse fuel
high temperature, low humidity, strong winds and dry fuel
low temperature, high humidity, light winds and moist fuel
high temperature, high humidity, still air and green fuel
questions.explanation: Bushfire behaviour depends on weather, fuel and topography. Hot, dry, windy days dry out fuel and drive flames forward, while high humidity and moist fuel slow a fire's spread.

questions.stem: A bushfire reaches the foot of a steep forested slope. Compared with its spread over flat ground, the fire will most likely:
options: stop at the slope, because forests on slopes hold more moisture
spread faster uphill, because flames preheat the fuel above them
slow down, because a fire cannot easily burn upwards against gravity
spread faster downhill, because burning debris rolls downslope
questions.explanation: Flames lean towards the fuel upslope, drying and heating it so it ignites sooner, so fires run faster uphill. Rolling debris can start spot fires below, but the main front moves fastest up the slope.

questions.stem: Flash floods differ from riverine floods mainly because flash floods:
options: build up slowly over weeks across a large catchment
are caused by high tides rather than by heavy rainfall
occur only on the wide floodplains of major rivers
rise within hours of intense rain over a small area
questions.explanation: Flash floods follow short, intense rainfall, often in small, steep or urban catchments, and give little warning. Slow-rising floods across large catchments, such as on the Murray, are riverine floods.

questions.stem: A paddock in a creek's catchment is replaced by roads, roofs and car parks. The most likely effect on floods in the creek downstream is:
options: a higher but later flood peak
a lower but earlier flood peak
a higher and earlier flood peak
a lower and later flood peak
questions.explanation: Hard surfaces stop rain soaking in, and drains carry runoff quickly to the creek, so more water arrives sooner. This is a way human activity compounds the flood hazard over time as cities grow.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a tsunami from a storm surge?
options: a tsunami is set off by sudden displacement of water; a surge by low pressure and onshore winds
a tsunami is set off by low pressure and onshore winds; a surge by an earthquake under the sea
a tsunami affects only the open ocean; a storm surge affects only coasts sheltered from storms
a tsunami is a hydro-meteorological hazard; a storm surge is a geological hazard of the coast
questions.explanation: Tsunamis are caused by sea-floor earthquakes, landslides or eruptions that displace a mass of water, so they are geological. Storm surges are raised by an intense storm's low pressure and strong onshore winds, so they are hydro-meteorological.

questions.stem: Cane toads were introduced to Queensland's cane fields in 1935 to control beetles. Their later spread across northern Australia is best explained by:
options: high breeding rates and a toxin that kills native predators that eat them
deliberate releases by state authorities in every part of northern Australia
a need for the cold, dry winters that are found across northern Australia
their success in eating the cane beetles, which then let toads spread out
questions.explanation: Cane toads breed prolifically, have few natural predators in Australia, and poison native animals such as quolls and goannas that eat them. They also failed to control the cane beetles they were introduced to eat.

questions.stem: Over recent decades, the bushfire risk to people on Melbourne's outer urban fringe has increased largely because:
options: planned burning has been banned in all of the state's national parks
more homes have been built in or beside bushland at the urban fringe
bushfires were unknown in Victoria before the twentieth century
eucalypt forests near Melbourne have become less flammable over time
questions.explanation: Risk depends on exposure as well as the hazard, and building homes at the interface between suburbs and bush puts more people and property in the path of fires. Victoria has a long history of major fires, and planned burning continues.

questions.stem: How did the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico differ in cause from the 1989 Exxon Valdez spill in Alaska?
options: it came from a blowout at an offshore drilling rig, not a grounded tanker
it came from an oil tanker that ran aground on a reef, not from a drilling rig
it was caused by a tsunami striking an oil terminal on the coast
it released oil into a freshwater lake rather than into the sea
questions.explanation: Deepwater Horizon was a drilling rig that exploded after a well blowout, releasing oil from the sea floor for months. The Exxon Valdez was a tanker that ran aground in Prince William Sound, a comparison of two similar technological hazards.

questions.stem: In hazard geography, the level of risk to a community depends on:
options: the category of hazard alone, since each category carries a fixed level of risk
the number of disasters in the region's past, regardless of change
the likelihood of a hazard event and the vulnerability of exposed people
the magnitude of the hazard event, whatever the people exposed to it
questions.explanation: Risk combines the chance of a hazard event with how exposed and vulnerable people and places are. A large event in an empty area poses little risk, while a moderate one can be disastrous for a vulnerable community.

questions.stem: In a flood-prone town, which is a social factor that raises residents' risk level?
options: the town's site on low land beside a large river
many elderly residents who live alone without a car
low incomes that leave households unable to insure
weak enforcement of the council's planning rules
questions.explanation: Age, isolation, disability and lack of transport are social factors that make it harder to prepare and evacuate. Low incomes are an economic factor, weak enforcement is political, and the town's low site is environmental.

questions.stem: A country has earthquake-resistant building codes, but corruption means they are rarely enforced. This is best described as which kind of factor raising risk?
options: cultural
environmental
geological
political
questions.explanation: Governance, regulation and corruption are political factors that shape how vulnerable buildings and people are. The earthquake itself is geological, but the failure to enforce codes is a human, political decision.

questions.stem: In 2010, Haiti was struck by a magnitude 7.0 earthquake and Chile by one of magnitude 8.8. Chile's earthquake released far more energy, yet loss of life was far greater in Haiti. The best explanation is:
options: Haiti's poverty, weak building standards and limited emergency capacity
Chile's earthquake was too deep below the surface to cause any damage
Haiti's earthquake is classified as a technological rather than natural hazard
Chile experienced no secondary hazards, such as a tsunami, after its earthquake
questions.explanation: Economic and political factors such as poverty, poorly built housing and weak institutions raised Haiti's vulnerability. Chile's earthquake did cause damage and a tsunami, but Chile had stronger building codes and greater capacity to respond.

questions.stem: Which is a cultural factor that could affect a community's level of risk from a hazard?
options: a shortage of funding for the regional emergency service
a steep, forested terrain surrounding the community's homes
a strong attachment to ancestral land that makes people reluctant to leave
a low rate of household insurance cover among the people living in the community
questions.explanation: Beliefs, traditions and ties to place are cultural factors that influence whether people move away from a hazard or evacuate. Insurance is economic, service funding is political and terrain is environmental.

questions.stem: Which is a social impact of a prolonged drought on a farming community?
options: falling water levels in farm dams and nearby streams
rising stress and mental health problems among farming families
lower farm incomes as crop yields fall and stock must be sold
loss of topsoil from bare paddocks through wind erosion
questions.explanation: Social impacts affect people's wellbeing, health and community life. Lower incomes are an economic impact, while topsoil loss and falling water levels are environmental impacts.

questions.stem: Seabirds coated in oil after a spill often die of cold because:
options: oil blocks the sunlight the birds need to digest their food
oil mats their feathers so they lose insulation and waterproofing
oil raises the temperature of the surface water so they cannot dive for food
oil dissolves the birds' feathers, which then fall out completely
questions.explanation: Feathers trap air to insulate and waterproof a bird; oil makes them clump, so cold water reaches the skin. Birds also swallow oil while preening, adding to the environmental impact of a spill.

questions.stem: The 2015 earthquake in Nepal destroyed several centuries-old temples in Kathmandu's Durbar Square. The loss of the temples as heritage and places of worship is best classed as:
options: a geological impact
a cultural impact
an environmental impact
a political impact
questions.explanation: Damage to heritage, sacred sites and traditions is a cultural impact. The loss of tourist income from those sites would be a separate economic impact.

questions.stem: After a large flood on the Murray, a geographer records two effects: (1) homes and roads damaged for weeks; (2) red gum wetlands refilled, with waterbirds breeding over the following seasons. Which statement is correct?
options: (1) is a short-term negative impact and (2) a longer-term positive impact
(1) is a long-term positive impact and (2) a short-term negative impact
both are realised negative impacts on the natural environment
both are potential impacts, as neither has yet taken place
questions.explanation: Damage to homes and roads is negative and immediate, while refilled wetlands and breeding events are positive and unfold over seasons. Both effects actually happened, so they are realised rather than potential impacts.

questions.stem: A town has been built on the lower slopes of a volcano that has not erupted for several centuries. For this town, an eruption is best described as:
options: a realised impact that the town has already suffered
a technological hazard caused by the town's location
a short-term positive impact on the town's farmland
a potential impact that has not yet been realised
questions.explanation: A potential impact is one that could happen; a realised impact has already occurred. Building in the hazard zone raises the town's exposure, but it does not turn the eruption into a technological hazard.

questions.stem: A GIS map shows that suburbs with the most flood insurance claims closely match those built on the lowest floodplain land. This is an example of:
options: a temporal distribution
a strong spatial association
a weak spatial association
a change in relative distance
questions.explanation: Spatial association is the degree to which two phenomena are similarly arranged over space; here the patterns closely match, so the association is strong. A temporal distribution would show how events are spread over time.

questions.stem: Two choropleth maps of a region show household income and the time taken to recover after a cyclone. Low-income areas closely match the areas of slow recovery. A geographer should conclude that:
options: the maps show the movement of recovery funds from wealthy areas to poor ones
there is a strong spatial association that suggests an interconnection to investigate
low income has now been proven to be the only cause of the slow recovery in the region
there is no spatial association, as income and recovery are measured differently
questions.explanation: Matching patterns show a strong spatial association and point to a likely interconnection, but they do not prove cause or rule out other factors. Phenomena measured in different units can still be spatially associated.

questions.stem: Which is an expected effect of climate change on the bushfire hazard in south-eastern Australia?
options: cooler summers that slow the drying of forest fuels
longer fire seasons with more days of dangerous fire weather
fewer dangerous fire days, as warmer air brings more rain
a shift of nearly all bushfires into the winter months
questions.explanation: Higher temperatures and drier conditions in southern Australia have lengthened fire seasons and increased dangerous fire weather days, as reported by the Bureau of Meteorology and CSIRO. This is an interconnection between climate change and a hydro-meteorological hazard.

questions.stem: How does sea-level rise from climate change interconnect with the storm surge hazard?
options: it raises the base sea level, so surges reach further inland
it lowers storm intensity, so surges become rarer and smaller
it turns storm surges into a geological rather than coastal hazard
it affects only tides, so storm surges stay exactly the same
questions.explanation: A storm surge adds to the existing sea level, so a higher base level lets surges flood land that was previously out of reach. This compounds coastal erosion and flooding risk in low-lying places.

questions.stem: Satellites with thermal sensors that detect bushfire hotspots are an example of:
options: a choropleth map
a field transect
remote sensing
a GNSS receiver
questions.explanation: Remote sensing gathers information about Earth's surface from a distance, such as by satellite or aircraft. Geoscience Australia uses satellite data to map hotspots so agencies can identify and track fires.

questions.stem: GNSS receivers fixed to the ground around a volcano are used mainly to detect:
options: the temperature of the lava flows during an eruption of the volcano
the chemical make-up of gases leaving the crater
the extent of ash clouds drifting downwind
small movements of the ground surface as magma rises
questions.explanation: GNSS (such as GPS) can measure millimetre-scale changes in position, so swelling of the ground as magma rises can be tracked. Gas chemistry and ash clouds are measured by other instruments and by satellites.

questions.stem: After a flood, an agency overlays a GIS layer of the flood's extent on a layer of property boundaries. This allows the agency to:
options: prevent the river from flooding those properties in the future
identify which properties were inundated and assess the damage
predict the exact date and height of the next flood in the area
measure the depth of every flooded house without any field visits
questions.explanation: Overlaying layers shows which features coincide in space, here the flooded area and the properties within it. GIS supports assessment and planning but cannot predict the exact date of a future flood or stop one.

questions.stem: A limitation of ordinary optical satellite images for assessing a flood while it is happening is that:
options: they cannot show water at all, only dry land surfaces
they can be taken only at night, when water is coolest
they show each house but never the whole flood extent
cloud cover can hide the ground, unlike radar imagery
questions.explanation: Optical sensors record reflected sunlight, so cloud during a storm or flood can block the view. Radar sensors send out their own signal, which passes through cloud, so agencies often use radar images during floods.

questions.stem: In the six-figure grid reference 457312 on a topographic map, the digits 457 give:
options: the height of the feature above sea level
the bearing from true north in degrees
the easting, read along the bottom or top of the map
the northing, read up the side of the map
questions.explanation: Grid references give eastings first and northings second. The easting is the vertical grid line value, read along the horizontal edge, with the third digit estimating tenths of the square.

questions.stem: On a 1:25 000 topographic map, two river gauges are 6 cm apart. What is the distance between them on the ground?
options: 1.5 km
15 km
4.2 km
questions.explanation: Each centimetre represents 25 000 cm, which is 250 m. So 6 × 250 m = 1500 m, or 1.5 km.

questions.stem: A river gauge has 59 years of annual peak flow records. A flood is ranked third highest. Using recurrence interval = (n + 1)/m, its recurrence interval is:
options: 60 years
180 years
20 years
about 19.7 years
questions.explanation: Here n = 59 and m = 3, so (59 + 1)/3 = 60/3 = 20 years. Leaving out the + 1 gives about 19.7, and 60 is the numerator before dividing by the rank.

questions.stem: A levee is built to protect a town from the 1% annual exceedance probability (or '1-in-100-year') flood. Which statement is correct?
options: after one such flood occurs, the town is then safe for the next 99 years
a flood of that size will occur exactly once every century
the town's levee can never be overtopped by any floodwater
a flood that exceeds it has a 1% chance of occurring in any year
questions.explanation: Annual exceedance probability is the chance of the flood being equalled or exceeded in any single year, so two such floods can occur in successive years. Larger, rarer floods can still overtop a levee built to this standard.
